title: The Deciding Factor for Personal Agents Isn't the Model — It's Memory and Proactivity
dek: The Today team believes models are approaching AGI and costs are falling tenfold every year, so the bottleneck has shifted to memory and proactivity; and a product that does proactivity badly just becomes another spammy push notification.
why: The two founders get very concrete about the engineering details of Personal Agents: how memory is stored, how proactivity is evaluated, why intent routing is a disaster. High information density, but the product is not yet validated.
who: Founders and product managers building AI applications and agent products, especially those currently wrestling with memory architecture, proactivity design, and intent routing schemes.
skip: The closing reflections and goodbyes after 1:36:16, which carry little information.

points.h: The model is no longer the bottleneck — cost is
points.body: Gao Ce previously worked on model infrastructure and vector databases, always writing code by hand, until a model release this February made him feel intelligence had taken a leap, to the point where he thinks coding has reached AGI level. His reasoning: if coding can still improve tenfold or eightfold every year, and cost falls tenfold every year following scaling law, then in a year or two there will be cheap intelligence on your phone that is stronger than an average person. So what Personal Agents lack is not model capability, but how to use it. This judgment determines that Today's product focus is not the model, but the harness and product design.

points.h: Serving people with lots of digital assets first is a tradeoff you have to make
points.body: Gao Ce explains why early users are always the extremely busy and the willing-to-tinker: for a Personal Agent to create value, the precondition is that you have left enough context in the cyber world. For someone who doesn't use email and has no online footprint, the Agent cannot quickly learn your profile and can only have you tell it bit by bit, making the onboarding threshold extremely high. That's why OpenClaw first took off among programmers, because they are at a computer every day and leave behind a lot of context. A product serving only high-net-worth individuals can't scale, but before the problem of unifying physical-world and online context is solved, you can only start here.

points.h: The opposite of Personal AI isn't office work — it's high delegation cost
points.body: Suki pushes back on the question "you're doing a personal agent, why are you also doing office work": the opposite of Personal AI is not work, nor office agents, but high delegation cost. In the past, delegating something to an agent meant giving it a lot of context, whereas this generation of products goes directly into your life, connects to your apps, knows your colleagues and your relationship network, and often can get something done in one sentence. Gao Ce adds that for most people, especially Chinese people, life and work are hard to separate, and the busier you are the blurrier the boundary, so generalising from life to work is easier than the reverse.

points.h: Big companies excel at big blitzes, not at seeing and persisting
points.body: Suki says that as far as she knows, Qwen and Doubao spotted the OpenClaw direction mid-year and explored it for a while, then quickly gave up. Her learning is that what big companies are best at is not seeing something and believing in it, but big blitzes and burning resources. Right now this direction has no PMF and a very small TAM; even at a 15% paid conversion rate, the user volume would still look like a small market to a big company — last year DingTalk was 4 billion, Feishu 3 billion, WeCom around 3 billion, and the three together are under 10 billion. So big companies usually wait until the TAM is big enough before investing regardless of cost.

points.h: Raising a bunch of Agents is emotional value, not efficiency
points.body: Last December Gao Ce himself raised three agents — a design chief, a product chief, and a project chief — and in the end he only wanted to chat with the project chief, because the context was all in one place and he didn't need to explain it over and over to three roles. He thinks multi-agent may be a false need on the consumer side; many people raising a bunch of crayfish are mostly after the emotional value of "I have a bunch of underlings doing work", but in actual use it wastes tokens — coordination between different roles also costs your tokens and money. The real value of multi-agent lies in two brains supervising each other, such as in evo and testing scenarios, but most personal agents' daily use doesn't need that.

points.h: The outbox has higher information density than the inbox
points.body: Suki describes a concrete rubric for memory construction: after Town gets email authorisation, the naive approach is to scan the inbox and outbox for clues, but the core observation is that the emails you send carry higher information density, because sending is done with intent, and you describe your intent clearly — for example, when you want to work with someone you introduce yourself first. The inbox is other people's intent toward you; the outbox is your intent toward others. Email is a protocol that dates back to the 1960s, with a lot of protocol and side-channel signals behind it, and whether you can capture those signals in the product is the difference in memory quality.

points.h: Proactivity is an open scenario — you can't run AB tests on it
points.body: Gao Ce contrasts work scenarios with proactivity: work scenarios are closed problems, like the benchmark Workbody open-sourced, where you're given a workspace and you're done when you're done, and right and wrong are easy to evaluate. But proactive is an open scenario that uses a lot of your incremental information, and the goal is highly subjective, personalised, and multi-dimensional, related to push frequency, quality, and even your mood that day. Early on, a product can't run GSP or AB tests to validate proactivity, and it will be very difficult in the future too, so it heavily tests the product lead's understanding of the world and information architecture — it's something engineered and product co-designed.

points.h: Stacking an intent model in front is an engineering disaster
points.body: Gao Ce on intent recognition: the traditional approach is to stack a small intent model in front and then dispatch to different large models by intent — for example, recognising a weather question and using a very small model. But the drawback is that intent maintenance gets harder and harder; as the product expands horizontally across intents, you may end up stacking thousands of intents, and products with strong generalisation like Doubao, Yuanbao, and Workbody are especially hard to maintain. Moreover, once you stack an intent model, the context seen below is fragmented, and how messages are shared across multiple sub-models is a big problem — for engineering it's quite a disastrous thing. Manus published a blog in July 2025 about a context-aware state machine, but didn't go into implementation details.

quotes.text: The opposite of personal AI is not work, not office agents — the opposite of personal AI is high delegation cost.

I hear a lot of people raising a bunch of crayfish, and really it's more about the emotional value of seeing them do work — that I have a bunch of underlings working for me. But if you actually use it, you'll find it's wasting your tokens.

My feeling now is that model generalisation isn't as strong as people imagine, so the value of the product manager is very large; and models are actually becoming more and more homogenised. Once models become infrastructure in the future, the value of the product, or the value of the product manager, I think will only grow.
I think in the short term everyone is indeed overestimating this field, but in the long term it may be underestimated — in the short term, I think it's very much overestimated.
